summary: Summarizes the TLV codepoints in use by the IS-IS routing protocol and its pending extensions, as used by several ISPs. It records which numbers are taken so that new extensions do not collide with them.

eli5.summary: Each kind of information in an IS-IS message has a number tag. This document is a list of which tags are already in use, so nobody picks the same one twice.

questions: what tlv codepoints does is-is use
where are is-is tlv numbers listed
which is-is tlv codes are reserved
subtitle: A shared list of which type numbers IS-IS routers already use, kept so new extensions do not collide.

tldr.problem: IS-IS messages carry data in Type, Length and Value blocks, and no central authority hands out the type numbers, so independent extensions could pick the same number.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists every TLV codepoint in use at the time, with its number, the packet types it appears in and where it is defined.
tldr.outcome: It is informational and explicitly not an authority. It says it may be replaced by some type of official registry.

today: RFC 3359 is Informational and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. The text itself says it may be replaced at any time by some type of official registry.

sections.title: Why a List of Codepoints
sections.content:
IS-IS is an interior gateway routing protocol, developed originally by OSI and used with IP extensions. Its messages hold information in TLV blocks: a type, a length and a value. The RFC says it describes codepoints in use by several ISPs for routing within their clouds, and covers the pending extensions too.

The point is to avoid future conflicts. The core protocol is specified by ISO, while the IP extensions come from the IETF IS-IS working group. ISO provides no numbering authority and IANA covers only IP-related code points, so the memo says no plausible central authority exists.
sections.eli5: Many people add new kinds of notes to the same message format. A shared list keeps two people from using the same label for different things.

sections.title: The Reserved TLV Table
sections.content:
The table has one row per TLV: its name, its value, whether it may appear in IIH (hello), LSP (link state) and SNP (sequence number) packets, and its status. Status says where the code comes from, such as ISO 10589, RFC 1195, RFC 2763 or an IETF-draft.

Examples are Area Addresses (1), Padding (8), Authentication (10), IP Int. Reach (128), Protocols Supported (129), Dynamic Name (137), IPv6 Intf. Addr. (232) and P2P Adjacency State (240). Two rows are vendor-specific (Lucent 66, Nortel 176 and 177), and DECnet Phase IV (42) is marked ancient. Code 133 is marked Illegal and not used.
sections.eli5: It is a big chart: each tag has a number, a name, and which kinds of messages may carry it.

sections.title: Assignment Procedures and Security
sections.content:
The document does not constitute or represent any standard or authority assigning TLV numbers. Assignment happens on a shared, informational basis between ISO, SIF and the IETF working groups. It is to be updated periodically, in the fashion of the Assigned Numbers practice, and may be replaced at any point by some type of official registry. It does not name documents using the codepoints and does not cover sub-TLV codepoints.

On security, the RFC says IS-IS security applies and no specific security issues are introduced.
sections.eli5: The list is a friendly notice board, not a rulebook. A real official list might replace it one day.

references.text: Reynolds, J., "Assigned Numbers; RFC 1700 is Replaced by an On-line Database", RFC 3232, January, 2002.
R. Callon. Use of OSI ISIS for Routing in TCP/IP and Dual Environments. INTERNET-RFC, December 1990.
